scenes.tts: Meselson and Stahl grew E coli on heavy nitrogen, so all of its DNA was heavy. Then they added ordinary nitrogen and let the cells grow. They spun the DNA in caesium chloride, where heavy, hybrid and light DNA settle in separate bands. After one generation, all of the DNA sat in a single band. It was halfway between heavy and light. Why halfway?

scenes.visual: A tall caesium chloride tube: one purple heavy band low down; then a single band appears halfway with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen, so all of its DNA was heavy. Then they added ordinary nitrogen and let the cells grow. They spun the DNA in caesium chloride, where heavy, hybrid and light DNA settle in separate bands. After one generation, all of the DNA sat in a single band. It was halfway between heavy and light. Why halfway?

scenes.tts: Three ideas could explain it. Conservative copying keeps the old double helix whole and builds a new one. Semiconservative copying gives each daughter one old strand and one new strand. Dispersive copying makes each daughter a patchwork of old and new pieces. Old strands are purple here, and new strands are blue.
scenes.visual: Three columns: a purple parent duplex copies into two daughters under each model.
scenes.narration: Three ideas could explain it. Conservative copying keeps the old double helix whole and builds a new one. Semiconservative copying gives each daughter one old strand and one new strand. Dispersive copying makes each daughter a patchwork of old and new pieces. Old strands are purple here, and new strands are blue.

scenes.tts: Now predict the first generation. Conservative copying gives a heavy band and a light band, and never a hybrid. The single hybrid band that was seen rules it out. Semiconservative copying predicts that hybrid band. So does dispersive copying. One generation cannot tell those two apart.
scenes.visual: Each model gets a tube with its predicted bands; a yellow line marks the observed hybrid band; conservative is crossed out in red.
scenes.narration: Now predict the first generation. Conservative copying gives a heavy band and a light band, and never a hybrid. The single hybrid band that was seen rules it out. Semiconservative copying predicts that hybrid band. So does dispersive copying. One generation cannot tell those two apart.

scenes.tts: So the second generation decides. Semiconservative copying splits each hybrid into one hybrid and one light molecule. That gives equal amounts of hybrid and light. If mixing is even, dispersive copying makes every molecule a quarter old. It predicts one band, a quarter of the way from light to heavy. Meselson and Stahl saw hybrid and light in equal amounts. Uniform dispersive copying is out.
scenes.visual: Two tubes: semiconservative shows hybrid and light bands of equal size, dispersive one band a quarter of the way down; observed matches the first, dispersive is crossed out.
scenes.narration: So the second generation decides. Semiconservative copying splits each hybrid into one hybrid and one light molecule. That gives equal amounts of hybrid and light. If mixing is even, dispersive copying makes every molecule a quarter old. It predicts one band, a quarter of the way from light to heavy. Meselson and Stahl saw hybrid and light in equal amounts. Uniform dispersive copying is out.

scenes.tts: Now count a third generation of semiconservative copying. Start with one heavy duplex. After one round there are two hybrids. After two rounds there are two hybrids and two light molecules. After three rounds there are two hybrids and six light molecules. The two heavy strands never multiply. So for semiconservative copying, that is twenty five percent hybrid, and seventy five percent light.
scenes.visual: Four rows of duplexes: 1 heavy, 2 hybrid, 2 hybrid + 2 light, 2 hybrid + 6 light; the two original purple strands are ringed; then 25 percent and 75 percent.
scenes.narration: Now count a third generation of semiconservative copying. Start with one heavy duplex. After one round there are two hybrids. After two rounds there are two hybrids and two light molecules. After three rounds there are two hybrids and six light molecules. The two heavy strands never multiply. So for semiconservative copying, that is twenty five percent hybrid, and seventy five percent light.

scenes.tts: Here is the catch. The average heavy content is the same in all three models. Only the way the label is shared among molecules tells them apart. So predict the bands, and look at the generation where the models disagree. Keep this rule. Each new helix holds one parental strand and one new strand.
scenes.visual: Three first-generation tubes with a yellow average mark at the same height; then a hybrid duplex with an old and a new strand labelled.
